modules.title: Marketing: from customer need to a plan
modules.summary: Customer needs, market segments, the marketing mix, and writing a plan.

sections.heading: Marketing creates an exchange
paragraphs: Marketing identifies needs and builds an offering that customers value enough to exchange money, time, or attention for. Advertising is one part of promotion; marketing also includes research, products, channels, pricing, selling, and customer relationships. A good product with the wrong distribution can fail even when its advertising is strong. Retailing sells to the final consumer, while marketing operates throughout the supply chain.

sections.heading: Choose a target and a position
paragraphs: A market is a group of potential customers with needs and the ability and willingness to buy. Segmentation divides it into useful groups: demographic, geographic, psychographic, or behavioral. Select a reachable target, then explain why its members should prefer your offer. Cultural influences, friends, income, perceived risk, and previous experience can change buying decisions. Business buyers also evaluate specifications, reliability, total cost, and approval procedures.

example.scenario: A bicycle shop can serve commuters or weekend mountain bikers. Its research finds nearby commuters dislike unpredictable repair times.
example.solution: Target local commuters and position the service around dependable same-day repairs. Set capacity and appointment policies before advertising that promise.

sections.heading: Build a coherent plan
paragraphs: Start with a situation analysis: internal strengths and weaknesses plus external opportunities and threats. State an objective with a metric, baseline, target, and deadline. Align product, price, place, and promotion with that objective; assign responsibilities and a budget. A strategy is the broad approach, while a tactic is a specific action. Research analysts, salespeople, merchandisers, and brand managers contribute different skills to the plan. Compare outcomes with targets and revise the action when evidence changes.
bullets: Common mistake: choosing everyone as the target makes messages and resource decisions vague.
Common mistake: treating sales growth as proof that one advertisement caused it; seasonality and price changes may also matter.

sections.heading: How retail models evolved
paragraphs: Retailing developed from local shops and markets into department stores, supermarkets, shopping centers, specialist chains, ecommerce, and integrated digital-and-physical experiences. These models coexist because customers value different combinations of convenience, assortment, advice, price, and trust. Self-service shifts some selection work to shoppers; specialty retail emphasizes expertise or a focused range.

Ecommerce takes orders online but still needs payment, inventory, service, and fulfillment. A marketplace connects buyers with multiple sellers; a direct-to-consumer brand sells without a traditional retailer. Subscription retail provides recurring deliveries under agreed terms. Omnichannel retail coordinates channels, such as online ordering with store pickup and consistent stock information; merely having both a website and shop does not guarantee integration.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into groups with shared characteristics or needs.
The distinct place an offering should occupy in a target customer’s mind.
Coordinated decisions about product, price, place, and promotion.

modules.title: Market research
modules.summary: Choosing a research method, checking data quality, and using the findings.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
paragraphs: A useful research question names the decision and the uncertainty: should a store add evening opening hours, and would enough customers use them? Secondary data already exists, such as sales records or government statistics. Primary data is gathered for the current question through interviews, surveys, observation, or experiments. Begin with relevant existing evidence, then collect new information where a gap remains. Check publication date, population, definitions, and collection method.

sections.heading: Match method to question
paragraphs: Interviews uncover reasons but do not establish how common a belief is. Observation shows behavior but may not reveal motives. A survey can estimate patterns if its sample represents the intended population; a voluntary social-media poll may overrepresent enthusiastic followers. Ask one neutral question at a time. Separate satisfaction, purchase intention, and actual behavior. Use consistent measurement periods and document missing responses rather than quietly removing inconvenient answers.

example.scenario: A store asks only lunchtime shoppers whether it should open later. Eighty percent say no.
example.solution: The sample excludes people unable to visit at lunchtime. Survey the target neighborhood at varied times and inspect evening online orders before concluding that later hours have no demand.

sections.heading: Use information responsibly
paragraphs: Marketing-information management continuously collects and organizes data for decisions; one research project addresses a particular question. Useful measures include transactions, average order value, returns, conversion, repeat visits, and stock availability. Compare segments and time periods using the same definitions. Collect only necessary personal information, explain its purpose, restrict access, and avoid publishing identifiable responses. Report uncertainty and limitations alongside the finding.
bullets: Common mistake: a large biased sample remains biased.
Common mistake: confusing correlation with causation; an experiment needs a meaningful comparison.
Practice: write a research question, select a method, and name the most likely source of bias.

terms.definition: Information collected specifically for the current research question.
Systematic distortion caused by who is included or excluded.
Desired actions divided by eligible visits or opportunities.

modules.title: Products and brands
modules.summary: Product ranges, brands, warranties, and product life cycles.

sections.heading: Manage the entire offering
paragraphs: A product can be a good, service, experience, or combination. Product/service management selects, develops, improves, and retires offerings to meet customer needs. A product mix contains all the lines a company offers. Width counts distinct lines; depth counts variants within a line. Bundling combines complementary items, but customers should understand the package price and what is optional. Grades classify quality levels; standards define consistent criteria.

sections.heading: Support the brand’s promises
paragraphs: A brand identifies an offering and creates expectations about it. Corporate branding concerns the organization; product branding concerns an individual offer. Position using attributes that matter to the target, such as convenience, reliability, service, or price. A feature describes what exists; a benefit explains its value to the customer. A warranty describes specified obligations if a product fails, while a guarantee communicates a promise whose exact terms still need checking.

example.scenario: A backpack has water-resistant fabric, a 15-liter capacity, and a repair promise covering faulty seams for one year.
example.solution: Water resistance is a feature; keeping schoolwork dry is a benefit. Explain the capacity honestly and show the written repair terms instead of implying every type of damage is covered.

sections.heading: Adapt across the life cycle
paragraphs: Introduction often requires awareness and trial; growth demands dependable capacity and differentiation; maturity emphasizes retention and efficiency; decline requires evaluation of repositioning or withdrawal. These stages describe market patterns, not a fixed calendar. Service experiences depend on employees and processes, so branding must extend beyond logos to delivery. Monitor quality, complaints, returns, safety, and customer expectations. Consumer protection and ethical obligations require accurate claims and appropriate disclosure.
bullets: Common mistake: assuming an attractive brand can compensate indefinitely for poor delivery.
Common mistake: adding variants without checking demand, inventory costs, or confusion.

terms.definition: The number of product lines offered.
The number of versions within a product line.
The experience and value customers are led to expect.

questions.explanation: Variants within one line increase product depth.

choices: Keeps your load lighter on the walk home

questions.explanation: Corporate branding builds an identity for the entire organization.

questions.explanation: A promise becomes credible through dependable experiences.

questions.explanation: New offerings generally need customers to understand and try them.

modules.title: Pricing, margins, and distribution
modules.summary: Pricing decisions, margin calculations, and distribution channels.

sections.heading: Understand price decisions
paragraphs: Cost-based pricing starts with costs; competition-based pricing examines alternatives; value-based pricing considers what customers believe the benefits are worth. Demand, capacity, objectives, competition, and legal or ethical constraints all matter. A high price can signal quality but cannot create quality by itself. Transparent terms matter: a mandatory charge should not be hidden until the last step. Discounts change both volume and contribution, so evaluate their financial effect.

sections.heading: Calculate with the right denominator
paragraphs: Markup on cost equals selling price minus cost, divided by cost. Gross margin percentage uses selling price as the denominator. Contribution per unit is price minus variable cost; it pays fixed costs before becoming operating profit. Break-even units equal fixed cost divided by unit contribution, rounded up when whole units are sold. Distinguish total revenue from profit and check whether a question asks for a percentage or dollar amount.

example.scenario: A ticket sells for $20, costs $8 per attendee to deliver, and the event has $600 in fixed costs.
example.solution: Contribution is $12 per ticket, so break-even is 600/12 = 50 tickets. The $12 difference is 150% markup on the $8 cost but 60% margin on the $20 price.

sections.heading: Choose a channel
paragraphs: A direct channel connects producer and buyer; an indirect channel uses intermediaries such as wholesalers, retailers, agents, or booking platforms. Intermediaries can provide assortment, storage, financing, discovery, and convenience. Evaluate reach, service, control, cost, data access, and customer preference. Technology can synchronize inventory and orders across channels. Channel conflict occurs when partners compete or disagree about price, territory, or responsibilities; clear agreements and consistent information reduce friction.
bullets: Common mistake: calling every intermediary unnecessary because it receives a fee.
Common mistake: using revenue instead of contribution in break-even calculations.
Practice: compare a direct website with a reseller using total service and fulfillment cost.

terms.definition: Selling price minus variable cost per unit.
An organization that helps move an offer from producer to customer.
The sales level at which total contribution equals fixed costs.

questions.prompt: An item costs $30 and sells for $50. Gross margin percentage is:
questions.explanation: The $20 gross profit divided by the $50 selling price is 40%.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs are $900 and contribution is $15 per unit. Break-even is:
questions.explanation: 900 divided by 15 equals 60 units.

questions.prompt: Which is an indirect channel?
choices: A grower selling at its own farm

questions.explanation: The retailer is an intermediary between producer and final buyer.

questions.prompt: Value-based pricing starts primarily with:
questions.explanation: It considers the value the customer associates with the offer.

questions.prompt: What should be checked before offering a large discount?
choices: Its effect on unit contribution and expected volume
questions.explanation: Discounts can increase volume while reducing the contribution available for fixed costs.

modules.title: Promotion, media planning, and measurement
modules.summary: Promotional tools, media planning, and ways to measure a campaign.

sections.heading: Select the right promotional tool
paragraphs: Advertising buys message placement; publicity earns media attention; public relations manages relationships and reputation; sales promotion offers a short-term incentive; personal selling uses direct interaction. Direct marketing reaches selected recipients with a response mechanism. Institutional promotion builds the organization’s image, while product promotion encourages demand for a specific offer. Integrating the mix means timing, claims, design, and customer experience support the same objective rather than contradicting one another.

sections.heading: Plan media around the audience
paragraphs: Reach is the number of distinct people exposed; frequency is how often they are exposed; impressions count total exposures. A media schedule states what runs, where, when, and at what cost. Compare geography, audience fit, accessibility, timing, creative format, and cost rather than price alone. Cost per thousand impressions, or CPM, equals media cost divided by impressions times 1,000. Click-through rate measures clicks divided by impressions, while conversion requires a defined desired action.

example.scenario: An event ad costs $120 and receives 30,000 impressions. A different ad costs $80 for 8,000 impressions.
example.solution: The CPMs are $4 and $10 respectively. The first buys cheaper exposure, but the second could still perform better if it reaches likely attendees and produces more qualified purchases.

sections.heading: Check claims and campaign results
paragraphs: Create a plan with objective, audience, message, channels, budget, schedule, and evaluation. For a loyalty program, explain qualification, reward, expiry, and privacy terms. Cross-promotion pairs complementary partners, but both must agree to responsibilities and message use. Endorsements and paid relationships need appropriate disclosure. Do not claim results that evidence does not support. Evaluate awareness, traffic, qualified actions, cost per acquisition, and retention according to the original goal.
bullets: Common mistake: treating impressions as unique people or guaranteed sales.
Common mistake: calling a paid placement independent publicity.
Common mistake: comparing campaign performance when the measurement windows differ.

sections.heading: Advertising claims and disclosures
paragraphs: Advertisements should be truthful, supported by evidence, and clear about material conditions. Disclose a paid endorsement or other material relationship so the audience can recognize the incentive. Permission to use a logo, photograph, music track, or likeness is distinct from simply crediting its creator. Evaluate sweepstakes, customer data, comparative claims, and direct messages against current official guidance before launch. The source library links to official guidance; exact legal requirements depend on the activity and jurisdiction.

terms.definition: The number of distinct people exposed to a message.
The average number of exposures per person reached.
Media cost per thousand impressions.

questions.explanation: A coupon offers a short-term purchase incentive.

modules.title: Advertising copy and visual communication
modules.summary: Advertising messages, layout, typography, and color choices.

sections.heading: Build a message hierarchy
paragraphs: An effective advertisement has a specific audience and action. A headline attracts the relevant reader, supporting copy explains a benefit with evidence, and a call to action states the next step. Distinguish a factual claim from an opinion and check whether the evidence actually supports it. Storytelling connects a recognizable problem with a credible change; it should not invent customer results or conceal important conditions.

sections.heading: Use design to guide attention
paragraphs: Contrast, alignment, repetition, proximity, balance, and whitespace make relationships visible. Group related information and establish a clear reading order. Typography includes typeface, size, weight, line spacing, and line length; decorative type should not obscure essential information. Color harmony can unify a composition, but use labels and contrast rather than color alone. RGB is used for screens, while print workflows often use CMYK; preview output in its intended medium.

example.scenario: A poster for a beginner repair workshop contains five equal-size headlines, pale yellow text, and no registration instruction.
example.solution: Choose one main benefit headline, add the date and location in a secondary tier, use readable contrast, and place a clear registration instruction last. Keep fine-print conditions readable.

sections.heading: Adapt without losing the brand
paragraphs: A consistent voice expresses the same personality across email, social posts, signs, and collateral. Adapt length, dimensions, captions, and action to each platform rather than copying an entire poster into every format. Email needs a truthful subject, readable opening, and clear next step. Social content needs context even when seen without sound. Use properly licensed illustrations and images, accurate captions, alternative text where supported, and proofread all dates and contact details.
bullets: Common mistake: confusing visual complexity with persuasive information.
Common mistake: assuming a digital color will reproduce identically in print.
Common mistake: shrinking text until everything fits instead of editing the message.

sections.heading: Typography, color, and drawing media
paragraphs: Serif type has small finishing strokes; sans-serif type omits them. Display faces emphasize personality, while body faces prioritize sustained reading. Kerning adjusts specific letter pairs; tracking changes spacing across a selection; leading is line spacing. Avoid stretching type or using many competing styles. Complementary colors sit opposite on a color wheel; analogous colors sit near one another. Harmony supports mood, but luminance contrast determines much of text legibility.

Vector artwork uses scalable paths and is useful for logos and diagrams. Raster artwork uses pixels and suits photographs or painted textures; enlarging a small raster image can reveal pixelation. Pencil, ink, paint, photography, and digital illustration offer different textures and production needs. For print, check effective resolution, bleed, safe margins, and printer specifications. For digital output, check responsive cropping, file size, color contrast, and readable text at the actual display size.

terms.definition: A visual order that shows what should be noticed first, next, and last.
A clear instruction for the desired next step.
The consistent personality and style of an organization’s communication.

modules.title: Retail stock, transactions, and inventory control
modules.summary: Receiving stock, tracking inventory, processing sales, and handling returns.

sections.heading: Receive and store accurately
paragraphs: Receiving compares delivered goods with the purchase order and packing slip. Count items, inspect damage, record discrepancies, and follow the procedure for accepting or rejecting stock. Label and route merchandise to the correct storage or sales-floor location; update records when it moves. Safe storage considers weight, temperature, security, access, and perishability. FIFO moves older stock first; expiry-sensitive stock may require first-expiry-first-out instead. Never block aisles or emergency access.

sections.heading: Track what actually exists
paragraphs: A perpetual system updates inventory as transactions occur; a periodic system uses counts at intervals. Physical counts verify the records because theft, breakage, recording mistakes, and returns can create discrepancies. Shrinkage is the difference between recorded and actual inventory, measured on a consistent cost or retail basis. Reorder planning considers sales rate, lead time, and safety stock. Report an out-of-stock promptly, check other locations, and record lost-demand information.

example.scenario: A store expects 120 mugs at $5 cost each but counts 114. Average demand is 10 per day and replenishment takes four days.
example.solution: The missing six mugs represent $30 of shrinkage at cost. Investigate transaction and receiving errors before assuming theft. A basic reorder point is 40 mugs plus the chosen safety stock.

sections.heading: Control transactions and movement
paragraphs: Prepare a cash drawer with an authorized starting float. Record each sale, tender, refund, and exchange under policy, then reconcile expected cash with the count. Separate authorization, handling, and reconciliation where possible. Never store unnecessary card details or share login credentials. Shipment choices balance cost, speed, reliability, tracking, handling needs, and environmental impact. Allocation decisions use location-level demand rather than dividing every shipment equally.
bullets: Common mistake: recording a return without checking whether it can safely return to available stock.
Common mistake: confronting a suspected shoplifter instead of following trained safety procedures.
Common mistake: treating book inventory as unquestionable after a mismatch.

terms.definition: Recorded inventory minus inventory actually present, on a consistent valuation basis.
The time between placing an order and receiving usable stock.
Inventory records continuously updated by transactions.

modules.title: Assortments, displays, and the retail experience
modules.summary: Choosing products, planning displays, and checking sales results.

sections.heading: Plan the assortment
paragraphs: Merchandising selects, buys, presents, and manages goods for the intended shopper. A buyer or merchandiser studies demand, quality, brand mix, price points, seasonality, supplier reliability, and available space. Assortment width is the range of categories; depth is the selection within each. Too little depth can frustrate target shoppers; too much can tie up cash and create slow-moving stock. Use sales and inventory databases to compare performance by category, location, size, and vendor.

sections.heading: Organize the selling environment
paragraphs: Visual merchandising includes store layout, lighting, signage, fixtures, and product presentation. A display is a specific arrangement within that larger experience. A planogram shows intended product placement and shelf allocation. Cross-merchandising places complementary products together, such as notebooks and pens, to solve a customer need. A focal point, balanced arrangement, readable signs, and clear prices guide attention; reachable products and uncluttered routes make the arrangement usable.

example.scenario: A school store stocks many novelty pen colors but frequently runs out of basic black pens. Its display hides prices behind the merchandise.
example.solution: Use category and size-level sales data to deepen the black-pen assortment, reduce weak variants, and place a visible price sign near a notebook-and-pen grouping. Monitor stockouts as well as sales.

sections.heading: Maintain and evaluate displays
paragraphs: Inspect displays for dust, empty positions, damage, outdated offers, incorrect prices, and unstable fixtures. Restock without creating hazards, rotate seasonal materials, and dismantle and store fixtures carefully for reuse. Compare sales, conversion, stock availability, and shopper movement before and after a change, while noting other influences. Retail careers include buying, merchandising, allocation, inventory analysis, store management, and ecommerce operations; digital retail still needs assortment and fulfillment decisions.
bullets: Common mistake: displaying only what looks attractive while ignoring availability and customer demand.
Common mistake: claiming a display caused higher sales without considering a simultaneous discount.
Common mistake: allowing decorative fixtures to obstruct accessible routes or product labels.

terms.definition: A diagram specifying merchandise placement and shelf allocation.
Presenting complementary items together.
The number of variants available within a product category or line.

modules.title: Ethical selling: needs, demonstrations, and objections
modules.summary: Understanding a buyer’s needs, demonstrating a product, and answering objections.

sections.heading: Ask about the buyer’s needs
paragraphs: Selling helps a buyer select an appropriate solution, rather than pressuring everyone into the same purchase. Establish rapport, ask open questions about needs and constraints, listen, then confirm understanding. Research accurate product specifications and company selling policies before making claims. A customer choosing shoes for occasional walking has different needs from a competitive runner; recommending the most expensive model without understanding that distinction can damage trust.

sections.heading: Demonstrate value and respond to objections
paragraphs: Translate features into benefits relevant to the buyer. A demonstration should show how the product works, invite appropriate interaction, and address limitations honestly. Objections reveal uncertainty about fit, value, timing, risk, or authority. Clarify the concern, acknowledge it, provide evidence, and check whether it is resolved. Do not invent capabilities, misrepresent scarcity, or guarantee results outside your control. Digital tools can show specifications and availability, but information still needs verification.

example.scenario: A shopper says a $40 reusable bottle costs too much and needs one that fits a narrow bag pocket.
example.solution: Ask about budget and pocket size. Demonstrate fit and durability, compare a suitable lower-priced option, and explain the actual warranty. The right result may be a cheaper product or no sale.

sections.heading: Complete the sale and follow up
paragraphs: A close asks for a decision after the needs and concerns have been addressed. Summarize the agreed solution, explain total price and terms, and offer a clear next step. Suggestion selling recommends a genuinely useful complement rather than an unrelated extra. Process the transaction and documentation accurately, confirm delivery or pickup, and explain support and returns. Follow up when appropriate and with permission. Service quality after the sale supports repeat business and the brand promise.
bullets: Common mistake: answering an objection before finding out what the buyer actually means.
Common mistake: treating a hesitant customer as a challenge to defeat.
Practice: explain one product feature, its customer-specific benefit, and a limitation.

terms.definition: Questions and listening used to identify the buyer’s situation and priorities.
A concern or uncertainty that may prevent a buying decision.
Recommending a relevant complementary product or service.

questions.explanation: Clarification reveals whether the objection concerns affordability, fit, or perceived value.

modules.title: Customer relationships, empathy, and CRM
modules.summary: Customer service, brand promises, and responsible use of customer records.

sections.heading: Listen and respond respectfully
paragraphs: A service mindset treats the customer’s goal as a problem to understand. Greet people appropriately, listen without interrupting, ask relevant questions, summarize the request, and explain the next step. Empathy means recognizing a person’s feelings and circumstances without pretending to agree with an inaccurate claim. Adapt pace, language, channel, and format to the individual instead of assuming preferences from their background. Ask before helping and accommodate access needs within authorized procedures.

sections.heading: Deliver the brand promise
paragraphs: A brand promise becomes real in moments of truth: a checkout, arrival, support request, delay, or return. Employees reinforce the organization’s image through accuracy, reliability, courtesy, and ownership. Anticipate likely needs, such as directions or an accessible format, but confirm rather than stereotype. Explain policies in plain language, including what can be done within the policy. Set realistic expectations for timing and communicate early when circumstances change.

example.scenario: A guest cannot read a small-print registration form and is worried about holding up the queue.
example.solution: Offer an available accessible format or private assistance, ask what works best, and preserve dignity. Do not announce the guest’s difficulty to the room or assume the reason for it.

sections.heading: Use CRM as a relationship tool
paragraphs: Customer relationship management combines processes and technology to maintain interactions over time. A useful record includes consent, relevant preferences, order or case history, the agreed action, owner, and follow-up date. Record facts and respectful descriptions rather than insults or speculation. Limit access, verify identity before disclosing account information, and do not collect unrelated sensitive details. CRM can prevent repeated explanations and missed promises, but it cannot replace thoughtful listening.
bullets: Common mistake: equating empathy with promising every requested remedy.
Common mistake: collecting personal information because a form happens to have a field for it.
Common mistake: giving a standard script without checking whether it answered the actual inquiry.

terms.definition: Recognizing another person’s perspective and feelings.
An interaction that shapes a customer’s judgment of the organization.
Processes and tools used to manage customer relationships and interactions.

questions.prompt: Which response best demonstrates empathy?
choices: I understand the delay disrupted your plans; let us review the options
questions.explanation: It recognizes the impact and moves toward an authorized solution.

questions.prompt: Which CRM note is most useful?
choices: Requested email updates; follow up Friday
questions.explanation: It records an actionable preference and commitment without judgment.
